intro: Six variations take a quiet E-major song through quick counterpoint and trills that fill both hands. At the end, Artur Schnabel has only the original sixteen bars left to play.

sections.label: Theme · A song in sixteen bars
sections.mNote: Two repeated halves, with a dotted rhythm in three

sections.label: Var 1 · The melody rises an octave
sections.mNote: The right hand sings above left-hand chords

sections.label: Var 2 · The hands trade short phrases
sections.mNote: Light exchanges alternate with a tender canon

sections.label: Var 3–5 · Racing lines, then interwoven voices
sections.mNote: Two-part Allegro, slower 9/8, then a fugato

sections.label: Var 6 · Repeated Bs become trills
sections.mNote: The beat fills with smaller and smaller notes

sections.label: Theme · The plain song returns
sections.mNote: Sixteen bars again, this time without repeats

relations.basis: The sixteen-bar theme has two repeated eight-bar halves; both excerpts lie in its first half and repeat. relations.basis: Both excerpts lie in the second eight-bar half of the opening theme and its written repeat. These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The plain theme returns
relations.basis: After the sixth variation, Beethoven restores the opening theme without the earlier variation figuration; the listening map places this return near 750 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.958, sustained 16 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 749 s (cache/form/beethoven-109-variations.txt, candidate 11; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A song in three
cues.text: Beethoven asks for Gesangvoll, mit innigster Empfindung — songfully, with the deepest feeling. The E-major melody leans on the second beat of its three-beat bar. Each half repeats: there is time to get to know these sixteen bars.
cues.evidence: Beethoven’s heading in the 1820 sonata; our translation. Breitkopf & Härtel, Werke, Serie 16 No. 153, printed p. 104, theme and repeat signs. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An octave higher
cues.text: The first variation lifts the melody an octave and gives it little flourishes. Below, the left hand places a bass note and then a chord, like the steps of a slow dance. Beethoven marks the tune molto espressivo.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 104–105, Variation I: Molto espressivo, melody an octave above the theme.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Maximiliane at the piano
cues.text: The sonata bears Maximiliane Brentano’s name. Beethoven has known her since childhood; in 1812 he gives the young pianist a short trio to encourage her playing. Nine years later, sending this sonata, he writes: “I see you all before me.”
cues.evidence: Beethoven to Maximiliane Brentano, Vienna, 6 December 1821; the letter and the earlier gift of Trio WoO 39 are reproduced and documented at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus109/.

cues.title: One hand answers another
cues.text: Leggieramente: lightly. The hands toss short figures between them, leaving tiny rests. A tender passage follows in which two right-hand voices imitate one another above steady left-hand quavers. Then Beethoven fits the two ways of playing together.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 105–106, Variation II; its three successive kinds of writing are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two hands in pursuit
cues.text: The third variation breaks into Allegro vivace, two racing lines in 2/4. The next slows into 9/8; the fifth gathers several voices into a fugato. E major holds through these changes of pace.
cues.evidence: Variations III–V, tempo and metre headings and contrapuntal writing: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._30_(Beethoven); Giovanni Biamonti’s account at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus109/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: B begins to tremble
cues.text: The final variation starts at the theme’s slow tempo, with repeated Bs above the tune. Crotchets become quavers, then triplets, then smaller notes still. The repetition turns into trills, while the melody keeps singing through the middle of the piano.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 110: Tempo primo del tema, cantabile, repeated B, successive subdivisions and trills.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trills in both hands
cues.text: Long trills bind the final variation together. Runs sweep above them, then pass into the left hand while the right keeps trilling. The pianist has to sustain a singing line inside all those quick notes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 110–112, final variation. This cue retains the established final-variation passage time.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The song comes home
cues.text: The trills subside, and the original theme returns in E major, marked cantabile. Its chords and dotted rhythm are plain again. This time the two halves go by once; a quiet chord closes the sonata.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 112: diminuendo and pp at the end of the trills, then the theme without repeat signs and a quiet E-major ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A repeated B above the song
transitions.from: Var 3–5 · Racing lines, then interwoven voices
transitions.how: The fifth variation’s fast fugato closes, and Tempo primo del tema restores the theme’s pace. Cut time changes to 3/4. E major remains, but the piano now sings in slow notes, with repeated B above the melody and a bass that moves once per beat. Those repeated notes will grow into the trills.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 109–110; Biamonti’s account of Variations V and VI at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus109/.

transitions.title: The trill releases the original theme
transitions.how: The right-hand trill drops into the middle of the keyboard as the left hand’s arpeggios grow quieter. Beethoven writes più dimin., then pianissimo. The trill ends; the bass settles on E and the original melody returns above it, cantabile, with its plain chords and dotted rhythm.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 112, the last systems of Variation VI and the restored theme. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Opus109.pdf

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
